name: Quilt Frame Maker
character: Frames, hoops, and floor stands built by hand in a woodshop: heirloom tools for hand-quilting kitchens.

sections.eyebrow: Hand-quilting frames, built to outlive the quilts
sections.title: Wood, clamps, and a lifetime of even tension

sections.heading: From the woodshop
sections.html:
Every frame starts as rough oak and one afternoon at the jointer. The rails are planed true, drilled with the same jig their grandfather drilled in 1998, and finished by hand with oil and wax that will not smell up a sewing room.

Nothing is glued that a screw can hold, so a frame can travel flat, be rebuilt in another kitchen, and tighten up again after twenty winters by the stove.

items.quote: We quilted on my mother's floor frame until the whole neighborhood had a side. It is on its third family now.
items.author: R., Lititz

items.quote: The lap hoop ended my thirty-year argument with my husband's armchair.
items.author: D., Coatesville

sections.heading: In the crate
sections.html: Every order ships with the frame or hoop, clamps sized to the rails, a canvas? a twill tacking strip already stapled, spare screws in a labeled envelope, and one sheet of instructions worth reading, written after the first fifty crates taught us what to say.

items.a: A screwdriver, a free hour, and one other pair of hands for the floor frames. The rails are numbered, the holes are drilled, and the instructions assume you have never done this.

items.q: Will it fit through my door?
items.a: The widest crate is the width of a standard door frame plus two inches, and it always goes in the long way first. Write with your doorway if you are unsure.

items.q: Can you sign or date a frame?
items.a: Yes. The underside carries the maker's mark anyway, and a dedication burned into the rail has made more than one anniversary.

sections.title: Caring for a frame
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Oil once a year, keep it off the radiator, and it will outlive the quilts you blame it for.

sections.heading: The short list
sections.html:
Wipe the rails with a dry cloth after long projects, especially where hands rest. Feed the wood a coat of the wax included in the crate once a year, and keep the frame away from heat vents and sunny windows, which are harder on oak than quilting is.

Ratchets want a drop of oil on their birthday. If a rail ever warps, which the shop has seen three times in twenty years, write first; most warped rails are actually loose clamps and tighten back true.

sections.title: About {{guild_name}}
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: One woodworker, two helpers, and a jig older than the apprentices.

sections.html:
The first frame was built for my wife's quilting bee when the shop frames they could buy kept loosening by spring. The bee ordered four more. The bee told two other bees, and the woodshop stopped building kitchen cabinets that year.

The same jig drills every rail, the same hands rub every finish, and every crate gets the maker's mark under the bottom rail where only the next generation will look for it.

items.quote: We bought the 1840 reproduction for the museum's hands-on room. It has survived eight hundred schoolchildren and still squares up true.
items.author: A historical society curator

sections.title: Order a frame
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Pick a size, pick a wood if you like, and get on the list. The current wait is about six weeks.

sections.heading: Woods and waits
sections.html: Oak is standard and always in the pile. Cherry and walnut are cut when the sawmill has them and cost what they cost; the quote will say. Half down holds your place on the list, and the balance is due when the crate is on the truck.
